en: Analysis of the Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of Knowledge 1.
Singlefold Matrix (Ekaka-mātikā)
The basis for knowledge in one way:

the five consciousnesses are not roots; they are rootless, dissociated from roots, conditioned, formed, immaterial, mundane, subject to taints, subject to fetters, subject to ties, subject to floods, subject to yokes, subject to hindrances, adhered to, and subject to clinging.
They are associated with defilement, indeterminate, having an object, non-mental factors, results of kamma, acquired and subject to clinging, neither defiled nor associated with defilement,

neither accompanied by initial application and sustained application nor devoid of initial application while possessing only sustained application, but rather devoid of both initial and sustained application;

they are not accompanied by rapture, are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation, do not have roots that are to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation, and are neither leading to accumulation nor leading to dispersal.
Neither-learner-nor-non-learner; limited; belonging to the sense sphere; not belonging to the fine-material sphere; not belonging to the immaterial sphere;
included within the mundane; not included within the supramundane;
indefinite; not leading to escape. They have arisen bases and arisen objects.
Having a pre-arisen basis, having a pre-arisen object;
having an internal basis, having an external object;
having an unmixed basis, having an unmixed object.
They have various bases and various objects.
They do not experience each other’s domain or objective field.
They do not arise without attention.
They do not arise through mental attention;
they do not arise in succession;
they do not arise neither before nor after one another.
They do not arise immediately one after another.
The five types of sensory consciousness are effortless.
By means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not discern any phenomenon other than the mere impact [of the object].
Immediately after the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not discern any mental state whatsoever.
By means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not assume any posture.
Immediately after the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not assume any posture whatsoever.
By means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not initiate bodily action or verbal action.
Immediately following the five types of sensory consciousness, one likewise does not initiate bodily action or verbal action.
By means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states.
Immediately after the five types of consciousness, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states.
One does not enter or emerge from meditative attainments by means of the five types of consciousness;
nor does one enter or emerge from them immediately after the five types of consciousness.
One does not pass away or arise by means of the five types of sensory consciousness.
One does not pass away or arise even immediately after the five types of sensory consciousness.
By means of the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not sleep, does not wake up, and does not see a dream.
Even immediately after the five types of consciousness, one does not sleep, does not wake up, and does not see a dream; this is wisdom that discerns the basis of things as they truly are.
Thus is the basis of knowledge by way of a single method.
2. The Twofold Matrix.
The basis for knowledge is twofold:
mundane wisdom and supramundane wisdom;
wisdom that can be understood by some and wisdom that cannot be understood by some.
Wisdom with taints; wisdom without taints.
Wisdom dissociated from the taints that is with taints; wisdom dissociated from the taints that is without taints.
Wisdom that is subject to fetters; wisdom that is not subject to fetters.
Wisdom dissociated from the fetters but subject to them; wisdom dissociated from the fetters and not subject to them.
Wisdom subject to the ties; wisdom not subject to the ties.
Wisdom dissociated from the ties but subject to them; wisdom dissociated from the ties and not subject to them.
Wisdom that conduces to the floods, and wisdom that does not conduce to the floods.
Wisdom that is dissociated from the floods but conduces to the floods, and wisdom that is dissociated from the floods and does not conduce to the floods.
Wisdom that conduces to the yokes, and wisdom that does not conduce to the yokes.
Wisdom dissociated from the bonds but conducive to the bonds; wisdom dissociated from the bonds and not conducive to the bonds.
Wisdom subject to the hindrances; wisdom not subject to the hindrances.
Wisdom dissociated from the hindrances yet subject to them; wisdom dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to them.
Wisdom that is adhered to; wisdom that is not adhered to.
Wisdom dissociated from the taints (āsava) that is adhered to; wisdom dissociated from the taints that is not adhered to.
Wisdom that is clung to (upādinnā); wisdom that is not clung to (anupādinnā).
Wisdom that is subject to clinging; wisdom that is not subject to clinging.
Wisdom that is subject to clinging while being dissociated from clinging; wisdom that is not subject to clinging while being dissociated from clinging.
Wisdom that is defiled; wisdom that is undefiled.
Wisdom dissociated from the defilements but subject to them; wisdom dissociated from the defilements and not subject to them.
Wisdom accompanied by applied thought; wisdom without applied thought.
Wisdom accompanied by sustained thought; wisdom without sustained thought.
Wisdom with rapture, wisdom without rapture.
Wisdom accompanied by rapture, wisdom not accompanied by rapture.
Wisdom accompanied by pleasure, wisdom not accompanied by pleasure.
Wisdom accompanied by equanimity; wisdom not accompanied by equanimity.
Wisdom pertaining to the sense sphere; wisdom not pertaining to the sense sphere.
Wisdom pertaining to the form sphere; wisdom not pertaining to the form sphere.
Wisdom pertaining to the formless realm; wisdom not pertaining to the formless realm.
Wisdom that is included within the mundane; wisdom that is not included within the mundane.
Wisdom that leads to liberation; wisdom that does not lead to liberation.
Wisdom that is fixed, wisdom that is unfixed.
Wisdom that has something superior to it, wisdom that is unsurpassed.
Wisdom that brings about the goal, wisdom whose goal has been accomplished.
Thus is the basis for knowledge by way of twofold division.
3. The Threefold Schedule:
The basis for knowledge by way of threefold division.
Wisdom consisting of reflection, wisdom consisting of hearing, and wisdom consisting of cultivation.
Wisdom consisting of giving, wisdom consisting of virtue, and wisdom consisting of cultivation.
Wisdom regarding higher virtue, wisdom regarding higher mind, and wisdom regarding higher wisdom.
Skillfulness regarding gain, skillfulness regarding loss, and skillfulness regarding means.
Wisdom that is a result of kamma, wisdom consisting of states that are subject to ripening, and wisdom consisting of states that are neither results nor subject to ripening.
Wisdom that is clung to and subject to clinging, wisdom that is not clung to but subject to clinging, and wisdom that is neither clung to nor subject to clinging.
Wisdom accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought; wisdom without applied thought and with sustained thought only; wisdom without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Wisdom accompanied by rapture; wisdom accompanied by pleasure;
wisdom accompanied by equanimity. Wisdom leading to accumulation; wisdom leading to dispersal; wisdom leading neither to accumulation nor to dispersal.
Wisdom of those in training, wisdom of those beyond training, and wisdom that is neither of those in training nor beyond training.
Limited wisdom, exalted wisdom, and immeasurable wisdom.
Wisdom with limited objects, wisdom with exalted objects, and wisdom with immeasurable objects.
Wisdom having the Path as its object, wisdom having the Path as its cause, wisdom dominated by the Path.
Wisdom that has arisen, wisdom that has not yet arisen, wisdom that brings about arising.
Wisdom that is past, wisdom that is future, wisdom that is present.
Wisdom having the past as its object; wisdom having the future as its object; wisdom having the present as its object.
Wisdom that is internal; wisdom that is external; wisdom that is both internal and external.
Wisdom having the internal as its object; wisdom having the external as its object; wisdom having the internal and external as its object.

Wisdom accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought is of three kinds: there is that which is resultant, there is that which is of a nature to produce resultants, and there is that which is neither resultant nor of a nature to produce resultants.
There is that which is clung-to and subject to clinging, there is that which is not clung-to but subject to clinging, and there is that which is neither clung-to nor subject to clinging.
There is that which is accompanied by rapture, there is that which is accompanied by pleasure, and there is that which is accompanied by equanimity.
There is that which leads to accumulation; there is that which leads to diminution; there is that which leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
There is that which pertains to those in training; there is that which pertains to those beyond training; there is that which pertains neither to those in training nor to those beyond training.
There is that which is limited; there is that which is exalted; there is that which is immeasurable.
There is that which has a limited object; there is that which has a sublime object; there is that which has an immeasurable object.
There is that which has the Path as its object; there is that which has the Path as its cause; there is that which has the Path as its predominance.
There is that which is arisen; there is that which is unarisen; there is that which is bound to arise.
There are [states] past, there are future, and there are present.
There are those with a past object, there are those with a future object, and there are those with a present object.
There are internal, there are external, and there are both internal and external.
There is wisdom that has an internal object, there is wisdom that has an external object, and there is wisdom that has both an internal and external object.

Wisdom that is without applied thought but with sustained thought is of three kinds: there is that which is resultant, there is that which is of a nature to produce resultants, and there is that which is neither resultant nor of a nature to produce resultants.
There is wisdom that is grasped and subject to clinging, there is wisdom that is not grasped but subject to clinging, and there is wisdom that is neither grasped nor subject to clinging.
There is that which leads to accumulation; there is that which leads to diminution; there is that which leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
There is that which pertains to those in training; there is that which pertains to those beyond training; there is that which pertains neither to those in training nor to those beyond training.
There is that which has arisen; there is that which has not yet arisen; there is that which is liable to arise.
There is wisdom that is past, there is wisdom that is future, and there is wisdom that is present.
There is wisdom that is internal, there is wisdom that is external, and there is wisdom that is both internal and external.

There is wisdom that is without applied thought and without sustained thought, which is resultant; there is wisdom that is of a nature to produce resultants; and there is wisdom that is neither resultant nor of a nature to produce resultants.
There is that which is grasped and subject to clinging; there is that which is not grasped but subject to clinging; there is that which is neither grasped nor subject to clinging.
There is that which is accompanied by rapture; there is that which is accompanied by pleasure; there is that which is accompanied by equanimity.
There is that which leads to accumulation; there is that which leads to diminution; there is that which leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
There are those pertaining to the trainee (sekha), there are those pertaining to the one beyond training (asekha), and there are those pertaining to neither the trainee nor the one beyond training.
There are those with limited objects, there are those with exalted objects, and there are those with immeasurable objects.
There are those with the Path as their object, there are those rooted in the Path, and there are those dominated by the Path.
There is that which has arisen; there is that which has not yet arisen; there is that which is liable to arise.

There is that which is past; there is that which is future; there is that which is present. There is that which has a past object; there is that which has a future object; there is that which has a present object.
There is [wisdom] internal, there is external, and there is both internal and external.
There is that which has an internal object, that which has an external object, and that which has both an internal and external object.

Wisdom accompanied by rapture, wisdom accompanied by pleasure, there is that which is fruition, that which is of a nature to produce fruition, and that which is neither fruition nor of a nature to produce fruition.
There is that which is acquired and subject to clinging; there is that which is not acquired but subject to clinging;

there is that which is neither acquired nor subject to clinging. There is that which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought; there is that which is without applied thought and has only sustained thought; there is that which is without applied thought and without sustained thought.
There is that which leads to accumulation; there is that which leads to diminution; there is that which leads to neither accumulation nor diminution.
There are those belonging to the trainee (sekha), there are those belonging to the one beyond training (asekha), and there are those belonging to neither the trainee nor the one beyond training.
There are limited (paritta), there are exalted (mahaggata), and there are immeasurable (appamāṇa).
There are those with limited objects (ārammaṇa), there are those with exalted objects, and there are those with immeasurable objects.
There is that which has the Path as its object; there is that which has the Path as its cause; there is that which has the Path as its predominance.
There is that which has arisen; there is that which has not yet arisen; there is that which is destined to arise.
There is that which is past; there is that which is future; there is that which is present.
There are [states] having the past as their object; there are those having the future as their object; there are those having the present as their object.
There are internal ones; there are external ones; there are internal-external ones.
There are those having the internal as their object; there are those having the external as their object; there are those having the internal-external as their object.
Wisdom accompanied by equanimity is of three kinds: there is that which is result, there is that which is subject to result, and there is that which is neither result nor subject to result.
There is that which is acquired and subject to clinging, there is that which is not acquired but subject to clinging, and there is that which is neither acquired nor subject to clinging.
There is that which leads to accumulation, there is that which leads to diminution, and there is that which leads to neither accumulation nor diminution.

There are those pertaining to the trainee (sekha), there are those pertaining to the one beyond training (asekha), and there are those that pertain neither to the trainee nor to the one beyond training.
There are limited (paritta), there are exalted (mahaggata), and there are immeasurable (appamāṇa).
There are those with limited objects (ārammaṇa), there are those with exalted objects, and there are those with immeasurable objects.
There is that which has the Path as its object; there is that which has the Path as its cause; there is that which has the Path as its predominance.
There is that which has arisen; there is that which has not yet arisen; there is that which is destined to arise.
There is that which is past; there is that which is future; there is that which is present.
There are [states] having the past as their object; there are those having the future as their object; there are those having the present as their object.
There are internal ones; there are external ones; there are internal-external ones.
There are those having the internal as their object; there are those having the external as their object; there are those having the internal-external as their object.
Thus is the basis for knowledge in three ways.
4. The Fourfold Schedule:
The basis for knowledge in four ways—
Knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma; knowledge conforming to the truths; knowledge of one possessing the path;

knowledge of one possessing the fruit. Knowledge of suffering; knowledge of the origin of suffering; knowledge of the cessation of suffering; knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Wisdom pertaining to the sense sphere; wisdom pertaining to the fine-material sphere; wisdom pertaining to the immaterial sphere; wisdom that is not included [within the realms].
Knowledge of the Dhamma, knowledge of inference, knowledge of the subsequent, and conventional knowledge.

There is wisdom that leads to accumulation and not to diminution; there is wisdom that leads to diminution and not to accumulation; there is wisdom that leads to both accumulation and diminution; and there is wisdom that leads to neither accumulation nor diminution. There is wisdom that leads to disenchantment and not to penetration;

there is wisdom that leads to penetration and not to disenchantment; there is wisdom that leads to both disenchantment and penetration; and there is wisdom that leads to neither disenchantment nor penetration.
Wisdom partaking of decline, wisdom partaking of stability, wisdom partaking of distinction, wisdom partaking of penetration.
The four analytical knowledges.
The four paths of practice.
There are four objects:
knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death, knowledge of the cessation of aging-and-death, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death.
Knowledge of birth … [and so on] …
Knowledge of existence … [and so on] … knowledge of clinging … [and so on] … knowledge of craving … [and so on].
Knowledge of feeling … [and so on] … knowledge of contact … [and so on] … knowledge of the six sense bases … [and so on].
Knowledge of name-and-form … knowledge of consciousness … knowledge of volitional formations,
knowledge of the origin of volitional formations, knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
Thus is the basis for knowledge by way of fourfold division.
5. The Fivefold Schedule:
The basis for knowledge by way of fivefold division—
Five-factored right concentration, five-knowledge right concentration.
Thus is the basis of knowledge in its fivefold way.
6. The Sixfold Matrix.
The basis for knowledge by way of sixfold division:
wisdom regarding the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Thus is the basis for knowledge by way of sixfold division.
7. The Sevenfold Schedule The basis for knowledge by way of sevenfold division:
seventy-seven bases for knowledge.
Thus is the basis for knowledge in seven ways.
8. The Eightfold Schedule:
The basis for knowledge in eight ways—
Wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits.
Thus is the basis of knowledge in eight ways.
9. The Ninefold Matrix.
The basis for knowledge in nine ways:
wisdom regarding the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling.
Thus is the basis for knowledge in nine ways.
10. The Decad on the Schedule The ten bases of knowledge by way of tenfold division:
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which powers the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahma.
Which ten?
Herein, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible—this too [is one of those qualities].
The Tathāgata possesses the power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma— past, future, and present— in terms of its basis and its cause.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma— past, future, and present— in terms of its basis and its cause:
this too is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading everywhere.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading everywhere— this too is a power of the Tathāgata,
by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership among the assemblies.
He roars the lion’s roar and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands the world with its many elements and various elements as it really is.
That the Tathāgata understands the world with its many elements and various elements as it really is—this too is a quality of the Tathāgata.
There is the power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the diversity of inclinations among beings.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the diversity of inclinations among beings— this too is a power of the Tathāgata,
by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals—
this too is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata stands in the place of the bull.
He claims [these things], he roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as they really are, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
That the Tathāgata understands, as they really are, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments...

He understands this; this too is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the recollection of past lives.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the recollection of past lives— this too is a power of the Tathāgata,
by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies,
and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the passing away and rebirth of beings.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the passing away and rebirth of beings— this too is a power of the Tathāgata,
by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, and roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies.
He sets in motion the Wheel of Brahma.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the destruction of the taints.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the destruction of the taints—this too is a power of the Tathāgata.
There is a power by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
These are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Thus is the basis of knowledge in ten ways.
The Schedule.
The Exposition.
1. Singlefold Exposition:

The five types of consciousness are only non-causes, only rootless, only dissociated from roots, only conditioned by conditions, only conditioned, only formless, only mundane, only subject to cankers, only subject to fetters, only subject to ties, and only subject to floods.
It is exclusively associated with the yokes, exclusively associated with the hindrances, exclusively adhered to, exclusively subject to clinging,

exclusively defiled, exclusively indeterminate, exclusively with an object, exclusively non-mental factors, exclusively result, exclusively acquired and subject to clinging, exclusively undefiled yet defiling,

exclusively neither with applied thought nor sustained thought, exclusively not without applied thought but with sustained thought only, exclusively without applied thought and without sustained thought, and exclusively not accompanied by rapture.
It is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation; it has as its cause that which is to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation;

it leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution; it is neither for those in training nor for those beyond training; it is limited; it belongs exclusively to the sense sphere, not to the fine-material sphere, nor to the immaterial sphere; it is included within the mundane, not the supramundane; and it is indeterminate.
It is indeed not leading to liberation; it is merely arisen, cognizable by mind-consciousness, impermanent, and overcome by aging.
The five types of consciousness have arisen bases and arisen objects; they arise when the base has arisen and the object has arisen.
They have pre-arisen bases and pre-arisen objects; they arise when the base has pre-arisen and the object has pre-arisen.
"Having internal bases and external objects": for the five types of consciousness, the bases are internal and the objects are external.
"Having undifferentiated bases and undifferentiated objects": they arise with respect to an undifferentiated base and an undifferentiated object.
"Having diverse bases and diverse objects": the base and the object of eye-consciousness are one thing, while those of ear-consciousness are another.
The basis and the object of nose-consciousness are one thing; the basis and the object of tongue-consciousness are another;
the basis and the object of body-consciousness are another.

They do not experience each other’s range and domain: ear-consciousness does not experience the range and domain of eye-consciousness, nor does eye-consciousness experience the range and domain of ear-consciousness.
The nose-consciousness does not experience the objective domain of eye-consciousness, nor does eye-consciousness experience the objective domain of nose-consciousness.
The tongue-consciousness does not experience the objective domain of eye-consciousness, nor does eye-consciousness experience the objective domain of tongue-consciousness.
The body-consciousness does not experience the objective domain of eye-consciousness, nor does eye-consciousness experience the objective domain of body-consciousness.
Of ear-consciousness … [and so on] … of nose-consciousness … [and so on] … of tongue-consciousness … [and so on] …
Eye-consciousness does not experience the range and domain of body-consciousness, nor does body-consciousness experience the range and domain of eye-consciousness.
Ear-consciousness does not experience the range and domain of body-consciousness, nor does body-consciousness experience the range and domain of ear-consciousness.
Nose-consciousness does not experience the range and domain of body-consciousness, nor does body-consciousness experience the range and domain of nose-consciousness.
Tongue-consciousness does not experience the range and domain of body-consciousness, nor does body-consciousness experience the range and domain of tongue-consciousness.
They do not arise without attention; they arise for one who attends. They do not arise without mental engagement; they arise for one who engages the mind.
“They do not arise in succession” means they do not arise one after another.
“They do not arise neither before nor after” means they do not arise simultaneously.

“They do not arise immediately following one another” means that ear-consciousness does not arise immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, nor does eye-consciousness arise immediately after ear-consciousness has arisen.
Immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, nose-consciousness does not arise; and immediately after nose-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness also does not arise.
Immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, tongue-consciousness does not arise; and immediately after tongue-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness also does not arise.
Immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness does not arise; and immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness also does not arise.
Of ear-consciousness …pe… of nose-consciousness …pe… of tongue-consciousness …pe…
Immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, eye-consciousness does not arise; and immediately after eye-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness also does not arise.
Immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, ear-consciousness does not arise; and immediately after ear-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness also does not arise.
Immediately after body-consciousness has arisen, nose-consciousness does not arise; and immediately after nose-consciousness has arisen, body-consciousness also does not arise.
Immediately after the arising of body-consciousness, tongue-consciousness does not arise; and immediately after the arising of tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness also does not arise.
The five consciousnesses are effortless (*anābhoga*); for the five consciousnesses there is no turning toward [the object], no effort, no attention, and no mental application (*manasikāra*).
"By means of the five consciousnesses one does not cognize any phenomenon" means that by means of the five consciousnesses one does not cognize any phenomenon whatsoever.
"Except for the mere falling [upon the object]" means except for the mere impact.

"Even immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not discern any phenomenon" means that even by the mind-element immediately following the five consciousnesses, one does not discern any phenomenon.
"One does not assume any posture by means of the five consciousnesses" means that by means of the five consciousnesses, one does not assume any posture.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.

Immediately after the five types of sensory consciousness, one does not assume any posture; thus, immediately after the five types of sensory consciousness, even by means of the mind-element, one does not assume any posture—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
“By means of the five consciousnesses, one does not initiate bodily action nor verbal action” means that by means of the five consciousnesses, one does not initiate bodily action nor verbal action.

“Immediately after the five consciousnesses, one does not initiate bodily action nor verbal action” means that immediately after the five consciousnesses, even by means of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), one does not initiate bodily action nor verbal action.
“By means of the five consciousnesses, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states” means that by means of the five consciousnesses, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states.

"Immediately after the five kinds of consciousness, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states" means that immediately after the five kinds of consciousness, one does not undertake wholesome or unwholesome states even by the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
"One does not enter or emerge by means of the five kinds of consciousness" means that one does not enter or emerge by means of the five kinds of consciousness.

"Immediately after the five kinds of consciousness, one also does not enter or emerge" means that immediately after the five kinds of consciousness, one does not enter or emerge even by the mind-element.
"One does not die or arise by means of the five consciousnesses" means that one does not die or arise by means of the five consciousnesses.
"One does not die or arise even immediately after the five consciousnesses" means that one does not die or arise even by means of the mind-element immediately following the five consciousnesses.
"One does not sleep, wake up, or see a dream by means of the five consciousnesses" means that one does not sleep, wake up, or see a dream by means of the five consciousnesses.

Immediately after the five types of consciousness, one does not sleep, does not wake up, and does not see a dream; immediately after the five types of consciousness, one does not sleep, does not wake up, and does not see a dream even by means of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
Such is wisdom as the manifestation of things as they truly are.
Such is the basis of knowledge in its singlefold division.
Singlefold.
2. Exposition of the Twofold:
Wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate within the three planes is mundane wisdom; wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is supramundane wisdom.
All wisdom is cognizable by something and not cognizable by something else.

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom associated with the taints (*sāsava-paññā*); in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from the taints (*anāsava-paññā*).

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom dissociated from the taints yet still associated with the taints; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from the taints and entirely free from the taints.

Wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate in the three planes is wisdom that is subject to fetters; wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is wisdom that is not subject to fetters.

Wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate in the three planes is wisdom that is dissociated from fetters yet subject to fetters; wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is wisdom that is dissociated from fetters and not subject to fetters.

Wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate in the three planes is wisdom that is conducive to the knots; wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is wisdom that is not conducive to the knots.

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom dissociated from the fetters but subject to the fetters; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters.
In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom subject to the floods; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom not subject to the floods.

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom dissociated from the floods but subject to the floods; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from the floods and not subject to the floods.
In the three planes, wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate is wisdom associated with the yokes; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from the yokes.

In the three planes, wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate is wisdom both dissociated from the yokes and subject to the yokes; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom both dissociated from the yokes and not subject to the yokes.
In the three planes, wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate is wisdom that is obstructive; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom that is non-obstructive.

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom dissociated from the hindrances but subject to them (*nīvaraṇiya*). In the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to them (*anīvaraṇiya*).

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom that is adhered to (*parāmaṭṭha*). In the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom that is not adhered to (*aparāmaṭṭha*).

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom dissociated from the taints of clinging (*parāmāsa*) but adhered to; in the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from the taints of clinging and not adhered to.

In the three planes, wisdom that is resultant is wisdom associated with clinging (*upādinnā paññā*). In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome; in the three planes, wisdom that is functional-indeterminate; and in the four paths and four fruits—this is wisdom not associated with clinging (*anupādinnā paññā*).

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom subject to clinging (*upādāniyā paññā*); in the four paths and four fruits, wisdom is wisdom not subject to clinging (*anupādāniyā paññā*).

In the three planes, wisdom that is wholesome or indeterminate is wisdom dissociated from clinging yet subject to clinging (*upādānavippayuttā upādāniyā paññā*); in the four paths and four fruits, wisdom is wisdom dissociated from clinging and not subject to clinging (*upādānavippayuttā anupādāniyā paññā*).

Wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate in the three planes is wisdom associated with defilement; wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is wisdom not associated with defilement.

Wisdom regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate in the three planes is wisdom dissociated from defilements yet associated with defilement; wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is wisdom dissociated from defilements and not associated with defilement.
Wisdom associated with applied thought is wisdom with applied thought; wisdom dissociated from applied thought is wisdom without applied thought.
Wisdom associated with investigation is wisdom with investigation; wisdom dissociated from investigation is wisdom without investigation.
Wisdom associated with rapture is wisdom accompanied by rapture; wisdom dissociated from rapture is wisdom unaccompanied by rapture.
Wisdom associated with rapture is wisdom conjoined with rapture; wisdom dissociated from rapture is wisdom not conjoined with rapture.
Wisdom associated with pleasure is wisdom accompanied by pleasure; wisdom dissociated from pleasure is wisdom not accompanied by pleasure.
Wisdom associated with equanimity is wisdom accompanied by equanimity; wisdom dissociated from equanimity is wisdom not accompanied by equanimity.

Wholesome and indeterminate wisdom of the sense sphere is wisdom of the sense sphere; wisdom of the fine-material sphere, wisdom of the immaterial sphere, and wisdom that is not included [in the realms] is wisdom not of the sense sphere.

In the case of wholesome and indeterminate states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), wisdom is wisdom of the fine-material sphere; it is not wisdom of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), not wisdom of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), not wisdom that is unbound (*apariyāpanna*), and not wisdom that is not of the fine-material sphere.

In the case of wholesome and indeterminate states of the immaterial sphere, wisdom is wisdom of the immaterial sphere; it is not wisdom of the sense-sphere, not wisdom of the fine-material sphere, not wisdom that is unbound, and not wisdom that is not of the immaterial sphere.
Wisdom regarding the wholesome and indeterminate states of the three planes is wisdom that is bound (*pariyāpanna*); wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is wisdom that is unbound.

Wisdom in the four paths is wisdom that leads to liberation; wisdom in the three wholesome planes, in the four resultant planes, and in the three functional-indeterminate planes is wisdom that does not lead to liberation.
Wisdom in the four paths is fixed wisdom; wisdom in the three wholesome planes, in the four resultant planes, and in the three functional-indeterminate planes is unfixed wisdom.
Wisdom in the three wholesome and indeterminate planes is surpassable wisdom; wisdom in the four paths and the four fruits is unsurpassable wisdom.
In this context, what is wisdom that brings about welfare?
It is the wisdom pertaining to the functional-indeterminate states when an Arahant arouses direct knowledge or arouses meditative attainment in the four planes;
it is the wisdom pertaining to the resultant states when direct knowledge has arisen or meditative attainment has arisen in an Arahant in the four planes.
Wisdom regarding the functional-indeterminate states of meditative attainment is wisdom that has made its object clear.
Thus is the basis for knowledge by way of twofold division.
This concludes the dyad.
3. Exposition of the Triads.
Therein, what is wisdom consisting in reflection (*cintāmayā paññā*)?

It is the wisdom regarding the spheres of work prescribed by yoga, or the spheres of craft prescribed by yoga, or the branches of knowledge prescribed by yoga; that is, the ownership of one’s actions (*kammassakatā*), or conformity with truth (*saccānulomika*), or [the contemplation] that "form is impermanent," or "feeling is impermanent," and so forth.

That one acquires, without having heard it from another, such a conformable acceptance, view, preference, inclination, outlook, and reflective acceptance of the Dhamma as: "Perception... volitional formations...
consciousness are impermanent"—this is called wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya-paññā*).
In this context, what is wisdom born of hearing (*sutamaya-paññā*)?

Whatever conformable acceptance, view, preference, inclination, outlook, or reflective acceptance of the Dhamma one acquires by hearing it from another—concerning the spheres of action prescribed by yoga, or the spheres of craft prescribed by yoga, or the fields of knowledge;

concerning the ownership of action, or that which accords with truth; or [the understanding] that form is impermanent, or feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is impermanent—this is called "wisdom consisting in what is heard."
All wisdom of one who has attained meditative absorption is wisdom consisting in development.
In this context, what is wisdom consisting in giving?
It is the wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises with reference to giving and is acquired through giving.
This is called "wisdom consisting in giving.
In this context, what is wisdom consisting in virtue?
It is the wisdom, the understanding, that arises based on virtue, attained through virtue... [and so on] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view.
This is called "wisdom consisting in virtue.
All wisdom of one who has attained meditative absorption is "wisdom consisting in cultivation.
In this context, what is wisdom regarding higher virtue?

The wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises in one who is restraining themselves with the restraint of the Pātimokkha—this is called "wisdom regarding higher virtue" (adhisīla-paññā).
In this context, what is "wisdom regarding higher mind" (adhicitta-paññā)?

The wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises in one who enters upon the attainment of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere—this is called "wisdom regarding higher mind.
In this context, what is "wisdom regarding higher wisdom"?
Wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits—
this is called "wisdom that is higher wisdom.
In this context, what is skill in acquisition?
“When one attends to these phenomena, unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, and arisen unwholesome states are abandoned.
Or, when one attends to these other phenomena, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states lead to increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment.
Whatever wisdom there is therein, understanding … [and so on] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called the faculty of wisdom.
This is called "skill in acquisition.
In this regard, what is "skill in avoidance"?
"When one attends to these phenomena, unarisen wholesome states do not arise, and arisen wholesome states cease."

"Or else, when one attends to these things, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen do arise, and unwholesome states that have already arisen lead to their increase and expansion"—the wisdom, understanding, ...
[as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view regarding this—that is called "skillfulness concerning the states of loss."
All wisdom regarding the means for that [attainment] is skill in means.
Wisdom regarding the ripening of results in the four planes is wisdom of the ripened state.
Wisdom regarding the wholesome in the four planes is wisdom of things subject to ripening.
In the three planes, wisdom regarding the functional-inefficient (kriyā-abyākata) is wisdom that is neither resultant nor subject to resultancy.
In the three planes, wisdom regarding the resultant (vipāka) is wisdom that is acquired and subject to clinging.
In the three planes, wisdom regarding the wholesome (kusala) and in the three planes, wisdom regarding the functional-inefficient, is wisdom that is unacquired but subject to clinging.
Wisdom in the four paths and the four fruits is wisdom that is neither-clung-to-nor-liable-to-clinging.
Wisdom associated with applied thought and sustained thought is wisdom with applied thought and sustained thought.
Wisdom dissociated from applied thought but associated with sustained thought is wisdom without applied thought and with sustained thought only.
Wisdom dissociated from applied thought and sustained thought is wisdom without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Wisdom associated with rapture is wisdom accompanied by rapture.
Wisdom associated with pleasure is wisdom accompanied by pleasure.
Wisdom associated with equanimity is wisdom accompanied by equanimity.
Wisdom in the three wholesome planes is wisdom leading to accumulation.
Wisdom in the four paths is wisdom leading to dismantling.
Wisdom regarding the resultants in the four planes and regarding the functional-indeterminate states in the three [upper] planes is wisdom that leads neither to accumulation nor to dismantling.
Wisdom in the four paths and in the first three fruits is the wisdom of the trainee (*sekha*).
The wisdom in the fruit of arhatship above that is the wisdom of the one beyond training (*asekha*).

Wisdom regarding the wholesome states of the three planes, the resultant states of the three planes, and the functional-indeterminate states of the three planes is wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Wisdom regarding the wholesome and indeterminate states of the sense-sphere is limited wisdom.
Wisdom regarding the wholesome and indeterminate states of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere is exalted wisdom.
In the four paths and the four fruits, wisdom is immeasurable wisdom.
Therein, what is wisdom with a limited object?
It is the wisdom that arises contingent upon limited phenomena; it is understanding … [as before] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
This is called "wisdom with a limited object.
In this context, what is wisdom with a sublime object?
It is the wisdom that arises contingent upon sublime states; it is understanding ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view.
This is called "wisdom having a sublime object.
In this context, what is wisdom having an immeasurable object?
It is the wisdom that arises with reference to immeasurable phenomena—the understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view.
This is called "wisdom with an immeasurable object.
In that regard, what is wisdom with the path as its object?
It is the wisdom, the understanding, that arises contingent upon the Noble Path... [as before] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view.
This is called "wisdom having the path as its object.
Wisdom regarding the four paths is wisdom with the path as its cause.
In this context, what is wisdom having the path as its dominant influence?

The wisdom that arises making the Noble Path its dominant influence—the understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called "wisdom dominated by the Path.
Regarding the wisdom in the result (vipāka) within the four planes: it may have arisen, it may be about to arise, and it should not be said that it has not arisen.
In the four planes, wisdom regarding the wholesome and in the three planes regarding the functional and the indeterminate may be arisen, may be unarisen, and cannot be said to be "bound to arise.
All wisdom may be past, may be future, or may be present.
In this regard, what is wisdom that has a past object?

The wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises with reference to past phenomena—this is called “wisdom having the past as its object.
In this context, what is wisdom having the future as its object?

The wisdom that arises with reference to future phenomena—the understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called "wisdom having the future as its object.
In this context, what is wisdom having the present as its object?

The wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises with reference to present phenomena—this is called "wisdom having the present as its object.
All wisdom may be internal, external, or both internal and external.
In this context, what is wisdom having the internal as its object?

That wisdom which arises contingent upon internal phenomena—the understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called "wisdom having the internal as its object."
In this context, what is wisdom having an external object?

It is that wisdom which arises with reference to external phenomena; it is understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called "wisdom having an external object."
In this context, what is wisdom having both internal and external objects?

It is the wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises with reference to phenomena both internal and external—this is called "wisdom having both internal and external objects."
Thus is the basis of knowledge in three ways.
The Triad.
4. The Exposition of the Tetrad.
In this regard, what is the knowledge of being the owner of one’s kamma?
It is: "There is what is given; there is what is sacrificed; there is what is offered; there is the fruit and result of wholesome and unwholesome deeds;
there is this world; there is the other world; there is mother; there is father; there are beings of spontaneous birth."

“There are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly and practiced rightly, who, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known”—such wisdom as this, such understanding ... [and so on] ...
non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
This is called "knowledge of one's own karma as one's own property.
With the exception of the knowledge that conforms to the truths, all wholesome wisdom associated with the taints is "knowledge of one's own karma as one's own property.
In this context, what is the "knowledge that conforms to the truths"?
“Form is impermanent,” or “feeling is impermanent,” ... perception ...

volitional formations ... or “consciousness is impermanent”—whatever such conformity, acceptance, view, preference, inclination, regard, and acceptance through contemplation of the Dhamma there may be—this is called “knowledge in conformity with the truths.”
Wisdom in the four paths is the knowledge of one possessing the path.
Wisdom in the four fruits is the knowledge of one possessing the fruit.

The knowledge of one possessing the path is knowledge regarding suffering, it is knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, it is knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and it is knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is knowledge regarding suffering?
It is the wisdom, the understanding, that arises with reference to suffering... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called "knowledge regarding suffering."

The wisdom, understanding, ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arise with reference to the origin of suffering, ... with reference to the cessation of suffering, ... and with reference to the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this is [wisdom].
This is called "knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Wisdom regarding wholesome and indeterminate states of the sense sphere is wisdom of the sense sphere; wisdom regarding wholesome and indeterminate states of the fine-material sphere is wisdom of the fine-material sphere;
wisdom regarding wholesome and indeterminate states of the immaterial sphere is wisdom of the immaterial sphere; [and wisdom] regarding the four paths and the four fruits [is supramundane wisdom].
Wisdom is wisdom that is not included [within the mundane].
Therein, what is knowledge of the Dhamma?
Wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits is knowledge of the Dhamma.
Thus, by means of this Dhamma—known, seen, attained, realized, and fully penetrated—he applies the method to the past and the future:

"Whatever recluses or brahmins in the past directly knew suffering, directly knew the origin of suffering, directly knew the cessation of suffering, and directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of suffering; [they all did so by means of this very Dhamma]."
They have directly known this very suffering; they have directly known this very origin of suffering;
they have directly known this very cessation of suffering; they have directly known this very path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Whatever recluses or brahmins in the future will directly know suffering, the origin of suffering...

“They will directly know suffering; they will directly know the origin of suffering; they will directly know the cessation of suffering; they will directly know the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
They will directly know this very suffering; they will directly know this very origin of suffering;
they will directly know this very cessation of suffering; they will directly know this very practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
The wisdom that is there, the act of understanding ... [as before] ... non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called "knowledge by inference.
In this context, what is "knowledge of the subsequent"?
Here, a bhikkhu, by means of his own mind, understands the minds of other beings and other persons.
He understands a mind affected by lust as "a mind affected by lust," and a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust";
he understands a mind affected by hatred as "a mind affected by hatred," and a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred."
He understands a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion," or he understands a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion";
he understands a contracted mind as "a contracted mind," or he understands a distracted mind as "a distracted mind"; or he understands a magnified mind as "a magnified mind."
He understands a non-exalted mind as "a non-exalted mind"; he understands a surpassable mind as "a surpassable mind";
he understands an unsurpassable mind as "an unsurpassable mind";
he understands a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind"; or he understands an unconcentrated mind...
“He understands an unconcentrated mind as ‘unconcentrated mind’; he understands a liberated mind as ‘liberated mind’;
or he understands an unliberated mind as ‘unliberated mind’”—whatever wisdom, understanding, ...
[and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view therein.
This is called "knowledge of comparison" (*pariyā-ñāṇa*).

Excluding knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhamma-ñāṇa*) and knowledge of inference (*anvaya-ñāṇa*), which are knowledge of comparison, all remaining wisdom (*paññā*) is conventional knowledge (*sammuti-ñāṇa*).
In this context, what is wisdom that leads to accumulation and not to diminution?
Wisdom in wholesome states of the sense sphere leads to accumulation, not to diminution.
Wisdom in the four paths leads to diminution, not to accumulation.
Wisdom in wholesome states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres leads both to accumulation and to diminution.
The remaining wisdom leads neither to accumulation nor to diminution.
In this context, what is wisdom that leads to disenchantment but not to penetration?
It is that wisdom by which one becomes free from lust for sensual pleasures, yet does not penetrate the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) nor the [Noble] Truths.
This is called "wisdom for the sake of disenchantment,
not for the sake of penetration. When one, being free from lust for sensual pleasures through that same wisdom, penetrates the direct knowledges but not the [noble] truths,
this is called "wisdom for the sake of penetration, not for the sake of disenchantment."
Wisdom regarding the four paths leads both to disenchantment and to penetration;
the remaining wisdom leads neither to disenchantment nor to penetration.
In this context, what is wisdom that partakes of decline?
When perceptions and mental applications accompanied by sensual desire occur in one who has attained the first jhāna, that is wisdom partaking of decline.
When mindfulness consistent with that state remains established, that is wisdom partaking of stability.
When perceptions and mental applications unaccompanied by directed thought occur, that is wisdom partaking of distinction.
When perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion occur, there is wisdom partaking of penetration.
When perception and attention accompanied by applied thought occur in one who has attained the second jhāna, there is wisdom partaking of decline.
The mindfulness that conforms to that state becomes established; this is wisdom partaking of stability.
When perception and attention accompanied by equanimity operate, it is wisdom partaking of distinction.
When perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion operate, it is wisdom partaking of penetration.
For one who has attained the third jhāna, when perception and attention accompanied by rapture and pleasure operate, it is wisdom partaking of decline.
When mindfulness conforms to that state, wisdom partaking of stability is established.
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by neither-pain-nor-pleasure prevail, wisdom partaking of distinction arises.
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by disenchantment prevail and are associated with dispassion, wisdom partaking of penetration arises.
When perception and attention accompanied by equanimity occur in one who has attained the fourth jhāna, that is wisdom partaking of decline.
When mindfulness in accordance with that state remains established, that is wisdom partaking of stability.
When perception and attention accompanied by the base of infinite space occur, that is wisdom partaking of distinction.
When perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion proceed, there is wisdom partaking of penetration.
When for one who has attained the base of infinite space, perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by form proceed, there is wisdom partaking of decline.
When mindfulness in accordance with that state becomes established, there is wisdom partaking of stability.
When perception and attention accompanied by the base of infinite consciousness occur, there is wisdom partaking of distinction.
When perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment occur, being associated with dispassion, there is wisdom partaking of penetration.
For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, when perception and attention accompanied by the base of infinite space occur, there is wisdom partaking of decline.
When mindfulness conforms to that state, it is wisdom partaking of stability.
When perceptions and mental orientations associated with the base of nothingness prevail, it is wisdom partaking of distinction.
When perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion prevail, it is wisdom partaking of penetration.
When perception and attention accompanied by the base of infinite consciousness occur in one who has attained the base of nothingness, that is wisdom partaking of decline.
When mindfulness conforming to that state remains established, that is wisdom partaking of stability.
When perception and attention accompanied by the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception occur, that is wisdom partaking of distinction.
When perceptions and mental orientations accompanied by disenchantment and associated with dispassion proceed, there arises wisdom that partakes of penetration.
In this context, what are the four analytical knowledges?
They are the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.

Knowledge regarding the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the doctrine is the analytical knowledge of the doctrine (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology therein is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
These are the four analytical knowledges.
In this context, what are the four modes of progress (*catasso paṭipadā*)?

Wisdom of painful practice with slow direct knowledge; wisdom of painful practice with quick direct knowledge; wisdom of pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge; wisdom of pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.
In this context, what is wisdom of painful practice with slow direct knowledge?

It is the wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, that arises in one who produces concentration with difficulty and effort, and who realizes the goal slowly.
This is called "wisdom that is difficult in its progress and slow in direct knowledge.
In this context, what is wisdom that is difficult in its progress and quick in direct knowledge?

It is the wisdom, the understanding, … [as before] … the non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view, that arises in one who produces concentration with difficulty and effort, yet quickly realizes its goal.
This is called "wisdom that is difficult practice with quick direct knowledge.
In this context, what is wisdom that is easy practice with sluggish direct knowledge?

It is the wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises in one who produces concentration without difficulty or exertion, but who realizes that state sluggishly.
This is called "wisdom that is pleasant in its progress and slow in direct knowledge.
In this context, what is wisdom that is pleasant in its progress and quick in direct knowledge?

It is the wisdom, the understanding, ... [and so on] ... the absence of delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view, that arises in one who produces concentration without difficulty or exertion and quickly realizes the goal.
This is called "wisdom with a pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge.
These are the four practices.
In this context, what are the four objects of focus?

Wisdom that is limited with a limited object; wisdom that is limited with an immeasurable object; wisdom that is immeasurable with a limited object; wisdom that is immeasurable with an immeasurable object.
In this context, what is wisdom that is limited with a limited object?

It is the wisdom, the understanding, ... [as above] ... the absence of delusion, the investigation of phenomena, right view, that arises in one who does not obtain concentration at will and who expands the object only slightly.
This is called "limited wisdom with a limited object.
In this context, what is limited wisdom with an immeasurable object?

It is the wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises for one who does not obtain concentration at will, but who pervades a vast object.
This is called "limited wisdom with an immeasurable object.
In this context, what is "immeasurable wisdom with a limited object"?

It is the wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises for one who has obtained concentration at will and who expands the object only slightly.
This is called "immeasurable wisdom with a limited object.
In that regard, what is immeasurable wisdom with an immeasurable object?

It is the wisdom, the understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises for one who has obtained concentration at will and who pervades a vast object.
This is called "immeasurable wisdom with an immeasurable object.
These are the four objects.

For one possessing the path, this knowledge regarding aging-and-death is knowledge; this knowledge regarding the origin of aging-and-death is knowledge; this knowledge regarding the cessation of aging-and-death is knowledge; and this knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death is knowledge.
In this context, what is knowledge regarding aging and death?

Whatever wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view arise with reference to aging and death—this is called "knowledge regarding aging and death."

The wisdom, understanding, ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises concerning the origin of aging and death, ... concerning the cessation of aging and death, ... and concerning the way leading to the cessation of aging and death—this is [wisdom].
This is called "knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of aging and death.
This knowledge of one who possesses the Dhamma is also knowledge of birth …pe… it is also knowledge of existence …pe….
This is knowledge regarding clinging …pe… this is knowledge regarding craving …pe… this is knowledge regarding feeling …pe…
This knowledge extends to contact …pe… this knowledge extends to the six sense bases …pe… this knowledge extends to name-and-form …pe…

This is knowledge regarding consciousness …pe… this is knowledge regarding volitional formations, this is knowledge regarding the origin of volitional formations, this is knowledge regarding the cessation of volitional formations, and this is knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
In this context, what is knowledge regarding volitional formations?

The wisdom, understanding, ... [as above] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view that arises with reference to volitional formations—this is called "knowledge regarding volitional formations.
[That which arises] with reference to the origin of volitional formations ... [as above] ... [is called knowledge regarding the origin of volitional formations].

With reference to the cessation of volitional formations …pe… with reference to the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations, whatever wisdom, understanding …pe… non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view arises—
this is called "knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations. –24
Thus is the basis for knowledge by way of fourfold division.
The Tetrad is finished.
5. The Exposition of the Pentad.
In this context, what is five-factored right concentration?
It is the pervasion by rapture, the pervasion by pleasure, the pervasion by the mind, the pervasion by light, and the sign of review.
Wisdom regarding two jhānas is the pervasion by rapture.
Wisdom regarding the three jhānas is the pervasion of happiness.
Knowledge of the minds of others is the pervasion of the mind.
The divine eye is the pervasion of light.
The knowledge of reviewing for one who has emerged from that or that concentration is the sign of reviewing.
This is called "right concentration with five factors.
In this context, what is right concentration with five kinds of knowledge?
“‘This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future’—such personal knowledge arises within him.
‘This concentration is noble and spiritual’—such personal knowledge arises within him.
‘This concentration is not practiced by base men’—such personal knowledge arises within him.”
“‘This concentration is peaceful, sublime, gained through tranquility, attained to unification, and is not constrained by exertion or forced,’ such knowledge arises within oneself.
‘Moreover, mindful I enter this concentration and mindful I emerge,’ such knowledge arises within oneself.
This is right concentration consisting of five kinds of knowledge.”
Thus is the basis of knowledge in five ways.
The Pentad is finished.
6. The Exposition of the Hexad.
In this context, what is wisdom regarding the six direct knowledges?

Knowledge of the various supernormal powers, knowledge of the purification of the divine ear-element, knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of recollecting past lives, knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and knowledge of the destruction of the taints— this is wisdom regarding the six direct knowledges.
Thus is the basis of knowledge in sixfold division.
The group of six.
7. The Exposition of the Sevenfold Division.
In this context, what are the seventy-seven bases of knowledge?
The knowledge that "with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death"; the knowledge that "in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death";
the knowledge that "in the past period also, with birth as condition, there was aging-and-death"; and the knowledge that "in the absence of birth, there was no aging-and-death."
The knowledge that "in the future too, with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death," and the knowledge that "in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death.
Furthermore, the knowledge that even this knowledge of the stability of phenomena is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation;
the knowledge that "with existence as condition, there is birth" ... [and so on].
Knowledge that "with clinging as condition there is existence" …pe… knowledge that "with craving as condition there is clinging" …pe… knowledge that "with feeling as condition there is craving" …pe…
Knowledge that "with contact as condition, there is feeling" …pe… knowledge that "with the six sense bases as condition,
there is contact" …pe… knowledge that "with name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases" …pe…

Knowledge that “with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form” …pe… knowledge that “with volitional formations as condition, there is consciousness” …pe… knowledge that “with ignorance as condition,
there are volitional formations,” and knowledge that “when there is no ignorance, there are no volitional formations”; [and so on] even regarding the past.
Knowledge that "in the past period, conditioned by ignorance, there were volitional formations"; knowledge that "if there were no ignorance, there would be no volitional formations";
knowledge that "in the future period, conditioned by ignorance, there will be volitional formations"; knowledge that "if there were no ignorance, there would be no volitional formations.

Furthermore, whatever knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) he has, he knows that too to be subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
These are the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
Thus is the section on the sevenfold basis of knowledge. The group of sevens is concluded.
8. The Exposition of the Eightfold (Aṭṭhakaniddesa).
Therein, what is wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits?

Wisdom regarding the path of stream-entry, wisdom regarding the fruit of stream-entry, wisdom regarding the path of once-returning, wisdom regarding the fruit of once-returning, wisdom regarding the path of non-returning, wisdom regarding the fruit of non-returning, wisdom regarding the path of arahantship, and wisdom regarding the fruit of arahantship.
This is wisdom regarding the four paths and the four fruits.
Thus is the basis of knowledge in eight ways.
The Octad.
9. Exposition of the Ninefold Set.
Therein, what is wisdom regarding the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling?
It is the wisdom of the attainment of the first jhāna, the wisdom of the attainment of the second jhāna, the wisdom of the attainment of the third jhāna... [and so forth].
Wisdom regarding the attainment of the fourth jhāna; wisdom regarding the attainment of the base of infinite space; wisdom regarding the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness;
wisdom regarding the attainment of the base of nothingness; wisdom regarding the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and the knowledge of reviewing for one who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is wisdom regarding these nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling.
Thus is the basis for knowledge in its ninefold aspect.
The section on the nines.
10. Exposition of the Ten Powers.
Therein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible?

Here, the Tathāgata understands: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any conditioned phenomenon as permanent; such a case does not exist. Thus he knows.
“He understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person might regard some conditioned phenomenon as permanent;
this is possible. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view might regard any conditioned phenomenon as pleasant;
this is not possible. He understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person might regard some conditioned phenomenon as pleasant; this is possible.’”
“He understands: ‘It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any phenomenon as substantial; such a case does not exist. He understands:
‘But it is possible, such a case exists, that an ordinary person should regard some phenomenon as substantial. He understands:
‘It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should deprive his mother of life; such a case does not exist.’”
“He understands: ‘It is possible that an ordinary person might deprive his mother of life; this is possible. He understands:
‘It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view might deprive his father of life...
[or] deprive an arahant of life...’”
One who, with a corrupt mind, sheds the blood of a Tathāgata … [or] causes a schism in the Saṅgha … [or] acknowledges another teacher … [would incur such a result].
He understands: "It is impossible, it cannot happen, that an ordinary person (puthujjana) should produce an eighth existence;
this is not possible. He understands: "But it is possible that an ordinary person might produce an eighth existence; this is possible. He understands:
"It is impossible, there is no occasion, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system; this is not possible."
He understands: "It is possible that in a single world-system one Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, might arise;

this is possible. He understands: "It is impossible, it cannot happen, that in a single world-system two Wheel-turning Monarchs (cakkavatti-rājāno) might arise simultaneously, neither before nor after the other;
such a thing is not possible. He understands: "But it is possible that in a single world-system one Wheel-turning Monarch might arise; this is possible."
“He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman should be an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible that a man should be an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha;
such a case does exist. He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a woman should be a Wheel-turning Monarch; such a case does not exist.’”
He understands: "It is possible that a man might be a wheel-turning monarch; this possibility exists. He understands:
"It is impossible, there is no occasion, for a woman to exercise the role of Sakka, to exercise the role of Māra, or to exercise the role of Brahmā; this possibility does not exist. He understands:
"But it is possible that a man might exercise the role of Sakka, might exercise the role of Māra, or might exercise the role of Brahmā; this possibility exists."
“He understands: ‘It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a desirable, agreeable, and pleasing result should arise from bodily misconduct; such a thing is not possible. He understands:
‘But it is possible that an undesirable, disagreeable, and unpleasant result should arise from bodily misconduct; such a thing is possible. He understands:
‘It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a desirable, agreeable, and pleasing result should arise from verbal misconduct... [and so on].”
He understands: "It is impossible that an agreeable, desirable, and pleasing result should arise from mental misconduct;

such a case does not exist. He understands: "But it is possible that an disagreeable, undesired, and unpleasant result should arise from verbal misconduct... [and] from mental misconduct; such a case does exist."
