“He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that an undesirable, unpleasing, or disagreeable result should arise from bodily good conduct; such a thing is not possible. He understands:
‘But it is possible that a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable result should arise from bodily good conduct; such a thing is possible. He understands:
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that an undesirable, unpleasing, or disagreeable result should arise from verbal good conduct... [and so on].”
He understands: "It is impossible that an undesired, unlovely, and disagreeable result should arise from good conduct of mind;

such a case does not exist. And he understands: "But it is possible that a desired, lovely, and agreeable result should arise from good conduct of speech... [and] from good conduct of mind; such a case does exist."

“He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who has engaged in bodily misconduct should, on that account and by reason of that, at the breaking up of the body after death, reappear in a happy destination, a heavenly world; such a case is not found. And he understands:

‘But it is possible that one who has engaged in bodily misconduct should, on that account and by reason of that, at the breaking up of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell; such a case is found.
‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who has engaged in verbal misconduct... [and so on].”

He understands: "It is impossible that one who possesses misconduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should, upon the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, a heavenly world; such a case does not exist. And he understands:
"But it is possible that one who possesses misconduct of speech...

[and] misconduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should, upon the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, hell; such a case does exist."

“He understands: ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who possesses good conduct of body, on account of that, with that as condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, should reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell;

such a case does not exist. He understands: ‘But it is possible, such a case exists, that one who possesses good conduct of body, on account of that, with that as condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, should reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world;
such a case exists. ‘It is impossible, it cannot happen, that one who possesses good conduct of speech... [and so on].”

He understands: "It is impossible that one who possesses good conduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should, after the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, or in hell; such a case does not exist. And he understands:
"But it is possible that one who possesses good conduct of speech...

[as before] ...or one who possesses good conduct of mind, on account of that and with that as condition, should, after the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; such a case exists."

“Whatever phenomena are causes and conditions for whatever phenomena, having depended [upon them], that is a possible case; whatever phenomena are not causes and are without conditions for whatever phenomena, having depended [upon them], that is an impossible case.

The wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view regarding this—that is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible, in accordance with reality.
In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge, in accordance with reality, of the results of past, future, and present karmic actions according to their basis and their cause?
Here, the Tathāgata understands:
"There are certain unwholesome undertakings of karmic action that, being obstructed by success in rebirth, do not ripen."
There are certain undertakings of evil kamma that do not ripen because they are obstructed by the excellence of one's acquisitions.
There are certain undertakings of evil kamma that do not ripen because they are obstructed by the excellence of the time.
There are certain undertakings of evil kamma that do not ripen because they are obstructed by the excellence of the means.
There are certain undertakings of unwholesome kamma that ripen by way of failure of destination;
there are certain undertakings of unwholesome kamma that ripen by way of failure of the physical basis;
there are certain undertakings of unwholesome kamma that ripen by way of failure of time.
There are certain undertakings of unwholesome actions that ripen due to a failure in their application.
There are certain undertakings of wholesome actions that do not ripen because they are obstructed by a failure in the destination (gati).
There are certain undertakings of wholesome actions that do not ripen because they are obstructed by a failure in the basis (upadhi).
There are certain wholesome undertakings of action that do not ripen because they are obstructed by a failure of time.
There are certain wholesome undertakings of action that do not ripen because they are obstructed by a failure of application.
There are certain wholesome undertakings of action that ripen by virtue of a favorable rebirth.
“There are certain undertakings of wholesome kamma that ripen depending on the excellence of the physical basis;
there are certain undertakings of wholesome kamma that ripen depending on the excellence of the time;
there are certain undertakings of wholesome kamma that ripen depending on the excellence of the application.”
The wisdom there, the understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, right view—
this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the result of the undertaking of kamma in the past, future, and present, according to its basis and its cause. In this context,
what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge as it really is of the way leading everywhere?
Here, the Tathāgata understands: "This is the path, this is the practice that leads to hell"; he understands:
"This is the path, this is the practice that leads to the animal realm"; he understands: "This is the path, this is the practice that leads to the sphere of hungry ghosts";
he understands: "This is the path, this is the practice that leads to the world of humans"; he understands: "This is the path, this...
He understands: "This is the path, this is the practice leading to the world of the devas"; he understands: "This is the path, this is the practice leading to Nibbāna.

The wisdom, the act of understanding, ... [and so on] ... the absence of delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view regarding this—that is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the practice leading everywhere as it really is.
In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the world as it really is, with its many elements and various elements?

Here, the Tathāgata understands the diversity of the aggregates, he understands the diversity of the sense bases, he understands the diversity of the elements, and he understands the diversity of the world with its many elements and various elements.

Whatever wisdom there is therein, understanding... [as before] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the world as it really is, with its many elements and various elements.
This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge, in accordance with reality, of the world with its many elements and its manifold elements.
In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge, in accordance with reality, of the diversity of inclinations among beings?
Here, the Tathāgata understands:
“There are beings who are inclined toward the inferior, and there are beings who are inclined toward the sublime.
Beings inclined toward the inferior associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings inclined toward the inferior.
Beings inclined toward the sublime associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings inclined toward the sublime.”

In the past, too, beings of inferior inclination associated with, frequented, and attended upon beings of inferior inclination; beings of sublime inclination associated with, frequented, and attended upon beings of sublime inclination.
In the future, too, beings of inferior inclination will associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings of inferior inclination;
beings of sublime inclination will associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings of sublime inclination.
...will attend upon [him].

Whatever wisdom there is therein, understanding ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the diversity of inclinations of beings as they really are.
In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge, in accordance with reality, of the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other persons?
Here, the Tathāgata understands the inclinations of beings, he understands their underlying tendencies, he understands their conduct, he understands their dispositions;

he understands those with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good character and those of bad character, and those who are easy to instruct and those who are difficult to instruct.
He understands beings who are capable and incapable of being instructed.
And what is the disposition of beings?
It is either: "The world is eternal," or "The world is not eternal," or "The world is finite," or "The world is infinite."

Or, "the soul is the same as the body," or "the soul is different from the body," or "a Tathāgata exists after death," or "a Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"— thus, these are based on views concerning existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*).
Or they are those who rely on the view of non-existence.
Or, having not approached either of these two extremes, there is obtained a conformable acceptance regarding dependently arisen phenomena—that is, knowledge as it really is.
This is the disposition of beings.
And what is the underlying tendency of beings? The underlying tendencies of beings are:

the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable, therein the underlying tendency to lust lies latent in beings.
Whatever in the world is unpleasant and disagreeable, therein the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent in beings.
Thus, with respect to these two things, they are beset by ignorance.
Conjoined with that [craving], conceit, views, and doubt are to be understood.
This is the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of sentient beings.
And what is the temperament (*carita*) of sentient beings?
The formation of merit, the formation of demerit, the formation of the imperturbable, whether belonging to a limited sphere or a vast sphere—
this is the conduct of beings.
And what is the inclination of beings?
There are beings who are inclined toward the inferior, and there are beings who are inclined toward the sublime.
Beings who are inclined toward the inferior associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings who are inclined toward the inferior.
Beings who are inclined toward the sublime associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings who are inclined toward the sublime.
In the past, too, beings who were inclined toward the inferior associated with, frequented, and attended upon beings who were inclined toward the inferior.
Beings who were inclined toward the sublime associated with, frequented, and attended upon beings who were inclined toward the sublime.
In the future, too, beings who are inclined toward the inferior will associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings who are inclined toward the inferior.
Beings who are inclined toward the sublime will serve, associate with, and attend upon beings who are inclined toward the sublime.
This is the inclination of beings.
Which are those beings who have great defilement?
There are ten bases of defilement:
greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread.
Those beings by whom these ten bases of defilement have been practiced, developed, cultivated, and brought to excess are beings with great defilements.
Which beings have little dust in their eyes?
Those beings for whom these ten bases of defilement have not been practiced, not cultivated, not made much of, and have not reached abundance—these are the beings who have little dust in their eyes.
Which beings have dull faculties?
There are five faculties:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Those beings for whom these five faculties have not been cultivated, developed, frequently practiced, and brought to maturity are beings of dull faculties.
Which beings have sharp faculties?
Those beings for whom these five faculties have been practiced, developed, cultivated, and brought to excellence—these are beings with sharp faculties.
Which beings are of two types?
Those beings who have evil intentions, evil underlying tendencies, evil conduct, and evil inclinations; who possess great defilement and dull faculties—these are beings of bad character.
Who are those beings of good character?
Those beings who have noble intentions, noble conduct, and noble inclinations; who possess little defilement and sharp faculties—these are beings of good character.
Which beings are difficult to instruct?
Those beings who are of two-fold character are the ones difficult to instruct.
Those beings who are of good character are the ones easy to instruct.
Which beings are incapable?
Those beings who are possessed of an obstruction of karma, possessed of an obstruction of defilements, and possessed of an obstruction of maturation;
who lack faith, lack aspiration, and lack wisdom; and who are incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness regarding wholesome states.
These beings are incapable.
Which beings are capable?
Those beings who are not possessed of an obstruction consisting of karma, not possessed of an obstruction consisting of defilements, and not possessed of an obstruction consisting of karmic fruition.
Those who are endowed with faith, possessed of zeal, and wise are capable of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states; these beings are capable.
Whatever therein is wisdom, understanding... [as before] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called the faculty of wisdom.
This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge, in accordance with reality, of the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals.

In this context, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge, in accordance with reality, of the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments?
One who is a meditator refers to four types of meditators.
There is a certain meditator who perceives prosperity as misfortune;
there is a certain meditator who perceives misfortune as prosperity; there is a certain meditator who perceives prosperity as prosperity;
and there is a certain meditator who perceives misfortune as misfortune.
These are four types of meditators.
There are another four types of meditators as well:

there is a certain meditator who enters attainment slowly but emerges quickly; there is a certain meditator who enters attainment quickly... [but emerges slowly]... [there is a certain meditator who enters attainment slowly and emerges slowly]... [and there is a certain meditator who enters attainment quickly and emerges quickly].
One emerges slowly; there is a certain meditator who enters attainment slowly and emerges slowly;
there is a certain meditator who enters attainment quickly and emerges quickly—these are the four types of meditators.
There are also four other types of meditators.
There is a certain meditator who is skilled in concentration regarding concentration, but not skilled in attainment regarding concentration;
there is another meditator who is skilled in attainment regarding concentration, but not skilled in concentration regarding concentration.
There is a certain meditator who is skilled in concentration regarding concentration and skilled in attainment regarding concentration;
there is another meditator who is neither skilled in concentration regarding concentration nor skilled in attainment regarding concentration—
these are the four types of meditators.
“Meditative absorptions” means the four meditative absorptions:
the first absorption, the second absorption, the third absorption, and the fourth absorption.
“Liberation”:
there are eight liberations.
Possessing form, one sees forms—
This is the first liberation.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally—
this is the second liberation.
He is intent only on the beautiful—
this is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space—
This is the fourth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness—
this is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving “there is nothing,” one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness—
this is the sixth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is the seventh liberation.
Having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling—
this is the eighth liberation.
“Concentration. There are three kinds of concentration:

concentration with applied thought and sustained thought, concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.
“Attainments”:
the nine successive dwellings in attainment—
the attainment of the first jhāna, the attainment of the second jhāna, the attainment of the third jhāna, the attainment of the fourth jhāna...

The attainment of the base of infinite space, the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the base of nothingness, the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
"Corruption" refers to states conducive to decline.
“Purification” means a state of dhamma that partakes of distinction.
“Emergence” means: purification is emergence, and emergence from this or that concentration is also emergence.

The wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view regarding those matters—this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of things as they truly are concerning the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditative absorptions (jhāna), liberations (vimokkha), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti).
In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of things as they truly are concerning the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati)?
Here, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes,
that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births,
twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, and even a hundred births.
“Even for a thousand births, or a hundred thousand births, or many aeons of world-contraction, or many aeons of world-expansion, or many aeons of both contraction and expansion, [I recall:
‘In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere.’”
"There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus one recollects one's manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
Whatever wisdom, understanding, ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view regarding this—this is called the power of the knowledge of recollecting past abodes.
This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of recollection of past lives as they really are.
In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings as it really is?

Here, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

“Indeed, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind; they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.”

"But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view—
upon the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination,

a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
The wisdom there, the understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—
this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings as it really is.
In this regard, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the destruction of the taints as it really is?

"Here, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon them.
Whatever wisdom there is therein, understanding... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the destruction of the taints as it really is."
The Tenfold Set.
The Analysis of Knowledge is finished.
